tweets.text:
It’s truly wild that we’re getting this level of performance from open models. Congrats to Kimi team on this.

Every time we lower the cost of frontier intelligence, the use-cases that enterprises can take on just go up. There’s a tremendous amount of workflows that enterprises would love to deploy that are only gated by the cost of tokens.

Importantly for the startup ecosystem, the combined breakthroughs from open and closed labs enable a ton of value to accrue to the layer, which can leverage a variety of models to complete full tasks for customers.

This diversity of models and approaches means that the applied AI layer can tune models to their workflows and route intelligence appropriately. Huge win for all.

Here’s another awesome use-case for what we can now do with our unstructured data because of AI agents. 

Box now works with Databricks so you can take structured data from enterprise content (like contracts, financial document, supply chain data) and connect that data into Databricks. 

This means that I can now query large document datasets without moving or reprocessing that content. And you can connect the data with any other system, like your ERP data, CRM, or product analytics. This opens up a ton of new use-cases for enterprise content. 

All possible because of headless software and agents.

builders.bio: Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.

tweets.text:
Open-weight models like Kimi and GLM will cause a complete rethink of the enterprise AI stack. 
If you are running an enterprise, you need to maximimize model optionality.
Here are 3 things you should be doing: 

1. Evals - build rigorous evals representative of your use case 
(a) Regression evals - tablestakes features that should always work with high reliability
(b) Aspirational / hill-climbing evals - harder use cases that the best model for your price point struggles to solve. So you scaffold it with prompting, context management and other techniques to overcome weaknesses or wait for a better model
These evals should be easy and quick to run. Eval velocity is a competitive advantage.

2. Model routing - Model selection is about tradiing off quality/cost/latency for your use case. If you have good evals, you know which models to route traffic to for different use cases.
This is something you ideally build yourself cos nobody understands your business and users like you do. 
There are off the shelf routers, but I haven't seen one I would recommend yet.
 
3. Model-agnostic harness - your system should never know which model is behind the API call.
This means your harness normalizes prompt structure, context management, tool definitions, and output parsing across models, making it easy to switch... once your evals pass.

长鑫科技打新，中一签能赚多少钱？

发行价 8.66 元，一签 500 股，中签后缴款 4330 元。

券商研报给出了四种估值情景：

市值达到 1 万亿元，一签大概能赚 3100 元；
市值达到 1.5 万亿元，一签大概能赚 6900 元；

聊聊长鑫科技董事长朱一明🧐🧐

长鑫科技上市在即，很多人开始问，朱一明到底是谁？

他是兆易创新创始人，也是长鑫科技董事长。

但这两个头衔，并不足以概括他的二十多年。

从公开资料里，关于朱一明个人生活的信息并不多。他几乎很少接受采访，也鲜少出现在公众视野。

从清华物理系毕业，到赴美从事芯片设计；从硅谷创业，再回到北京清华科技园创办兆易创新；最后，又一头扎进全球竞争最激烈的 DRAM 赛道。朱一明几乎踩中了中国半导体产业发展的每一个关键节点。

1️⃣朱一明出生于1972年，先后获得清华大学学士、硕士学位，并在美国纽约州立大学石溪分校取得硕士学位。毕业后，他曾在美国iPolicy Networks、Monolithic System Technologies等公司从事芯片设计工作。

2️⃣2004年，兆易创新的故事在硅谷起步。

2005年，朱一明带着团队回国，把总部放到北京清华科技园。彼时中国芯片设计行业还很早，DRAM和NAND这种大品类，技术、资金、产能，哪一项都不是一家初创公司能轻松碰的。

3️⃣于是，他选择了一条更「窄」的路——NOR Flash。

这并不是当时最大的市场，却拥有丰富的产品形态，更适合轻资产的Fabless公司切入。后来朱一明也解释过，当时的思路很简单：不跟国际巨头正面硬碰硬，而是先找到一条能够突破的缝隙。

4️⃣2008年，兆易推出自主设计的SPI NOR Flash。随后又陆续布局32位MCU、SPI NAND等产品，一步步从一家存储芯片公司成长为平台型半导体企业，并于2016年登陆上交所。

这段经历，也为后来挑战 DRAM 打下了基础。朱一明并不是一开始就在做 DRAM。他先在竞争相对没那么激烈的细分市场完成了产品、客户、供应链和资本市场的积累，再选择进入全球门槛最高、投入最大的存储芯片战场。

5️⃣2018年，他进入长鑫存储管理层，先后担任董事、董事长、CEO；2021年起担任长鑫科技董事长，带领长鑫不断向国际 DRAM 巨头发起挑战。

不过，也必须说明，长鑫从来不是一个人的故事。

它的背后，有合肥多年的持续投入，有国家大基金和产业资本的支持，更有数以千计工程师十余年的坚持。

朱一明或许是那个最具代表性的名字，但真正托起长鑫的，是一整个中国存储产业的长期投入与集体攻坚。

builders.bio: playing long-term games with long-term people

tweets.text:
i'm scared

in about a month, i'm launching an app.

i've spent seven months building it in silence, and i truly believe it can improve the life of hopefully millions of people.

i've also never done anything like this in my life.

day 1 of building in public i guess

honest thing first: starting over in a field where you have zero experience is scary.

i spent almost a decade in crypto. i knew every corner of that game.

in this one i knew nothing. not how apps make money, not what a paywall should look like, not why people come back. blank page, every day.

what helped more than anything: listening to people who've already walked it.

easily over 300 hours of founder interviews so far, mostly the revenuecat and superwall podcasts (s/o @JosephKChoi and @drbarnard, absolute GOATs).

one or two episodes, every single day, for months. it's the closest thing to borrowed experience that exists.

half of what i know about this business came from strangers talking into microphones. thank you, genuinely.

my biggest learning so far:

the product is maybe a third of the work. the rest is a machine most people never see.

onboarding, paywall, app store screenshots, aso, notifications, streaks.

a dozen levers that decide whether anyone ever finds the thing, tries it, pays for it, comes back.

nobody told me that, so i'll be telling you. that's what this series is: one lever at a time, what i try, what the numbers say.

and i'm not doing this alone anymore. there are people now working extremely hard to bring the app's content to life. more on them soon.

this is not me teaching. i'm not qualified to teach.

it's me learning in public, and you're welcome to tag along.

the app stays unnamed for now, but will share more soon

if you're starting something you have no experience in too, tag along.

it's less scary with company.

with love, Pix.
